extracted.intended_audience: customs brokers, continuing education providers, potential accreditors, and the trade community
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory standards and implementation rules for a continuing broker education program requiring customs brokers to complete accredited continuing education credits and maintain records, including accreditation, credit calculation, reporting, proration, and recordkeeping procedures tied to triennial status reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of continuing broker education requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: All individual brokers holding an active customs broker license must certify completion of the continuing broker education requirement when submitting their triennial status report, with two limited caveats: if an individual has not held a license for an entire triennial period or if an individual license is voluntarily suspended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule applies to any individual holding an active customs broker license regardless of employer, specialization, or whether they are 'actively engaged' in transacting business; exceptions for prorated requirements apply when the license was not held for the full triennial period or is voluntarily suspended (see prorating rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: 36-credit requirement per triennial period
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual brokers are required to complete 36 continuing education credits of qualified continuing broker education over the three years of a triennial period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CBP considers 36 credits over three years reasonable and attainable and notes it is easily prorated; the credits may be completed at any time during the triennial period and brokers may choose topics relevant to their practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triennial reporting dates and certification timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The 36-month cycle ends on January 31 and begins on February 1 every three years, coinciding with the triennial status report due February 1 of reporting years; brokers must certify completion of continuing broker education with the filing of their triennial status report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brokers may file earlier than the due date but must ensure they have completed the required credits in the shortened timeframe; CBP does not have discretion to alter the statutory triennial reporting period specified in 19 U.S.C. 1641(g).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date and transitional credit reduction for first period
rubrics_metrics.description: The first triennial reporting period that will require certification closes January 31, 2027, with the status report due February 1, 2027; CBP will reduce the number of required credits for the 2024–2027 period by six credit hours for approximately every six months that elapse between February 1, 2024 and the announced compliance date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CBP will announce the compliance date in a Federal Register notice following publication of the final rule; subsequent triennial periods require the full 36 credits unless an exception applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: No carryover of excess credits between triennial periods
rubrics_metrics.description: CBP does not allow individual brokers to carry over any continuing education credits completed in one triennial period in excess of the 36-hour requirement into the subsequent triennial period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prohibition is intended to ensure brokers maintain a current knowledge base by completing training within each three-year cycle; credits earned after the last day of January count only for the next cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prorating for partial-license periods and voluntary suspension
rubrics_metrics.description: If an individual has not held an active customs broker license for an entire triennial period or is reactivating a voluntarily suspended license, the required number of credits will be prorated at one continuing education credit for each complete remaining month until the end of the triennial period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prorated calculation is set out in 19 CFR 111.102(b) and applies in limited scenarios only (partial-period license holders and voluntary suspensions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a continuing education credit and half-credit allowance
rubrics_metrics.description: One continuing education credit equals one continuous hour of qualifying continuing broker education; CBP adopted half-credit units so that a 30-minute continuous participation period may award a half credit, and additional half credits are awarded for each full 30-minute segment thereafter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualified continuing broker education may award half a credit for 30 minutes of continuous participation; the final rule revises prior proposals to permit half-credit trainings and to allow instructors/discussion leaders/speakers to claim half a credit for each full 30 minutes spent presenting or preparing for a presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit assignment based on predetermined continuous participation, not actual individual attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility for credits is based on the amount of continuous participation designated for the activity (predetermined by the accreditor), not on the actual minutes an individual broker happened to participate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 45-minute activity counts as half credit; breaks, pauses, technical issues, or excess Q&A do not change the credited amount; CBP or CBP-selected accreditors will pre-approve the continuing education credit for each qualified activity so brokers know credits before participating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualified continuing broker education must be government-created or accredited
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualified continuing broker education must either be created by the government or accredited by a CBP-selected accreditor; only qualified trainings or educational activities provide continuing education credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Until CBP selects accreditors and accredits trainings, there are no qualified trainings; CBP envisions that many existing reputable private programs (e.g., CCS) may be accredited in the future but cannot be assumed qualified without formal accreditor evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: CBP-selected accreditors: selection process and obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: CBP will select accreditors through a contracting-type process (SAM) following an RFI and RFP; selection will result in a binding agreement between CBP and the selected party, and accreditors will be vetted for capability and required to meet standards and periodic renewal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No private party will be automatically designated an accreditor without review; the RFI/RFP process is intended to be transparent and to produce multiple qualified accreditors; the SAM process will be used and normal RFI/RFP procedures apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: CBP will not itself act as the accreditor
rubrics_metrics.description: CBP will not become an accreditor because it believes a public-private partnership is necessary and CBP lacks capacity to vet all trainings; CBP will, however, retain oversight and visibility into accredited trainings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CBP will institute a framework for the trade community to inform CBP of issues and will require limitations and requirements on accreditors to protect confidential business processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accreditation transparency and periodic renewal
rubrics_metrics.description: CBP intends the RFI/RFP application process to be transparent and intends that CBP-selected accreditors should be required to renew their accreditor statuses on a periodic basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should carefully review and respond to RFIs and RFPs; deficient proposals will be handled through the normal RFI/RFP processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping responsibility and minimum data elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual brokers must maintain records of qualified continuing broker education completed for three years after certifying completion and the records must meet the criteria of §111.102(d)(1) (title, provider, date, credits, location, and documentary evidence of registration/attendance/completion or similar).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Records may be physical or electronic; a transcript or similar electronic certification will suffice if it connects each credit to the six criteria; brokers remain responsible for maintaining records even if kept in an employer's LMS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility in record formats and storage location
rubrics_metrics.description: CBP intends for brokers to have flexibility in maintaining records in whatever format/location is convenient (including employer learning management systems) so long as the records meet §111.102(d)(1) and can be produced timely upon request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CBP will accept electronic or physical evidence; for online trainings the record location may simply be recorded as 'online.' However, ultimate responsibility for producing records rests with the individual broker.

rubrics_metrics.name: CBP record request procedures and response timeframe
rubrics_metrics.description: CBP may request continuing education records to ensure compliance; CBP added a 30-calendar-day timeframe from the date of receipt of CBP's record request for brokers to provide documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CBP will work with brokers to accommodate production methods and timeframes; the 30-day timeframe aligns with general recordkeeping requirements in 19 CFR part 163 and may include onsite or electronic production as feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Providers are not required to submit records to CBP on behalf of brokers
rubrics_metrics.description: CBP will not place a requirement on accredited providers to send records directly to CBP because provider-held records are not easily usable or collatable and such a system is susceptible to failure outside broker control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The recordkeeping burden is placed on brokers because they are best positioned to collate credits from multiple providers and ensure compliance; CBP disagrees that provider-submitted records would be administrable or beneficial for compliance purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brokers' freedom to choose training topics
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulations do not mandate specific trainings or topics (e.g., ethics); individual brokers are permitted and encouraged to choose trainings based on their needs and specialization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing brokers to choose topics provides flexibility recognizing that not every topic is equally relevant to every broker's practice area; this choice supports the goal of keeping brokers current in their specific practice areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accreditor evaluation of existing private certifications (e.g., CCS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing private programs (such as the Certified Customs Specialist certification) are not automatically qualifying; whether such certifications meet the continuing education requirement depends on future evaluation by CBP-selected accreditors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Until accreditors are selected and specific trainings evaluated, CCS or similar certifications cannot be used to meet the requirement; CBP envisions accreditors may determine such programs qualify given their reputations, but formal accreditation is required first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program scale and participating entities
rubrics_metrics.description: CBP will not limit the number of participating entities (accreditors/providers) and intends the program to involve as many parties as necessary to provide a wide range of trainings and topics while remaining manageable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To minimize confusion, CBP allows brokers to certify completion via their triennial status report and requires brokers to maintain their own records; CBP will provide CBP-identified free qualified alternatives to ensure low-cost/flexible options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accreditation enables standardization to address time variances
rubrics_metrics.description: Accreditation is intended to standardize how many continuing education credits are rewarded from any given activity, and will allow for technical difficulties, breaks, etc., to be accounted for and measured consistently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CBP declined to implement a 55-minute credit hour rule and instead relies on the accreditation process to standardize credit awards across government and private offerings.
